items.abstract: <jats:p>Certifying a per-event miss-risk floor for an energy-gated video pipeline costs n_req = ln δ/ln(1−ε) labeled events — the exact-binomial certification wall, 59 events at ε = δ = 5%. We ask whether conformal risk control (CRC) breaks it, and build the missing instrument: a per-event miss loss that couples the gate&apos;s schedule into the loss, a sliding-window online CRC with a closed-form update, and an adaptive risk budget ported from adaptive conformal inference. We prove one-step validity, a drift bound with a recovery guarantee, an assumption-free long-run bound, and an impossibility result across drift points. Replaying a 3,713-event detection-grounded corpus (121 videos, 3 datasets), stationary and under dataset-shift drift, returns a two-sided verdict. On sample count the wall falls: CRC certifies the 5% floor from 20 events against 59, a 2.95× reduction, with both theoretical thresholds confirmed to the event. On guarantee strength it stands: the cheaper certificate controls expected risk only, exceeding α in 31–44% of deployments even in the exchangeable control arm. The deepest finding is that the binding constraint is video-level exchangeability, not sample size: across 20 redrawn deployment splits neither framework reaches its nominal guarantee at 2,000 calibration events. The wall relocates rather than collapses. Under drift the sliding window is both safer and cheaper than a frozen certificate (risk 0.0446 against 0.0696; activation 0.716 against 0.846), a closed-form rule k_max(w) = ⌊α(w+1)−1⌋ predicts all 5 measured window breakpoints, and on-device calibration costs 10.98 μs and 7.67 μJ per event.</jats:p>
title: Online Conformal Risk Control for Streaming Detection under Frame Skipping and Drift

items.abstract: <jats:p>​Time series anomaly detection is critical for industrial system reliability and security. Existing methods typically operate at a single prediction scale, missing anomalies that manifest across different time horizons. We propose a Transformer-based framework combining temporally aligned multi-scale prediction, cross-scale consistency, and a variance-calibrated fusion rule with no learned parameters or per-dataset tuning of 𝛼. All horizons (1, 5, 10, 20, and 30 steps) forecast the same current state from causal contexts ending at the corresponding lags; a consistency signal measures disagreement among the same-target forecasts and flags anomalies that break cross-scale agreement. On 28 SMD server machines, under an identical EMA post-processing applied to every method, our method attains an average AUROC of 0.878, comparable to the best classical baseline (0.883), and the numerically highest AUPRC (0.494). On the HAI 21.03 industrial control system dataset, under a uniform causal evidence aggregation applied to every method, it attains the highest point-wise AUROC, F1, AUPRC, and range-based VUS-PR (0.857, 0.656, 0.504, and 0.591, with F1 at the exact oracle-optimal threshold). The same architecture template and all non-dimensional model and training hyperparameters are used across both domains, with each domain trained separately; only the causal score-aggregation rule is adapted to each dataset’s temporal characteristics. Batched GPU inference scores test windows in parallel without changing the computed anomaly scores. Case studies suggest that multi-scale prediction captures sudden failures (short horizons) and gradual drifts (long horizons),and that cross-scale consistency contributes a consistent improvement on both datasets.​​</jats:p>
title: Multi-Scale Transformer for Time Series Anomaly Detection Across Server and Industrial Control Domains ​

items.abstract: <jats:p>Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) in Industrial Control Systems (ICS) exploit vulnerabilities across operational layers, leveraging stealthiness mechanisms that make them fundamentally difficult to detect using single-domain approaches. While multi-domain anomaly detection has shown promise, existing studies focus on single-stage attacks, leaving realistic APT scenarios largely unexplored, partly due to the inability of companies to release representative operational data. This work addresses that gap by deploying an Electrical Power Monitoring System (EPMS), an industrial control system that measures electrical parameters across facility infrastructure integrating multiple industrial protocols, in collaboration with an industrial partner, and subjecting it to realistic APT campaigns to provide the multi-domain labelled data needed to study ICS-specific APT detection under operationally representative conditions. This paper presents three contributions: (i) a structured analysis of ICS-specific APTs establishing taxonomies of detection mechanisms, stealthiness mechanisms, and operational impact from documented real-world campaigns, directly informing the design of the dataset that follows; (ii) EPMS-APT&apos;26, the first labelled dataset of realistic ICS-specific APT campaigns collected from a physical three-layer testbed built in collaboration with an industrial partner, capturing multi-stage kill chains across both network and physical domains; (iii) a systematic benchmarking of single-domain and multi-domain anomaly detection approaches across SWaT&apos;16, SWaT&apos;19, and EPMS-APT&apos;26. Our evidence-grounded conclusions on the conditions under which existing approaches succeed or fail provide practitioners and researchers with a principled basis for selecting detection strategies. Results indicate that existing approaches exhibit significant limitations when faced with realistic ICS-specific APT campaigns, pointing to fundamental gaps in current detection methodologies.</jats:p>
title: Multi-Domain Anomaly Detection for Advanced Persistent Threat Detection in Industrial Control Systems

items.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid evolution of Industrial Control Systems (ICS) and Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) networks has significantly increased the exposure of critical infrastructure to sophisticated cyber threats. Traditional cybersecurity measures often struggle to address the unique challenges posed by these systems, such as data privacy, scalability, and real-time threat detection. Federated learning, a decentralized machine learning paradigm, has emerged as a promising solution to enhance security in ICS/SCADA environments. By enabling local model training on distributed devices while maintaining data privacy, federated learning offers a secure, scalable, and efficient framework for real-time anomaly detection and collaborative threat mitigation. This chapter explores the integration of federated learning with edge computing to address the computational and resource constraints of Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) devices, ensuring low-latency responses to emerging threats. The chapter further discusses the advantages of federated learning in enabling secure data sharing, improving system resilience, and complying with stringent data privacy regulations. With applications spanning predictive maintenance, intrusion detection, and threat intelligence, federated learning represents a pivotal advancement in securing ICS/SCADA networks. This chapter provides a comprehensive analysis of the role of federated learning in modern industrial cybersecurity, highlighting its potential to transform the landscape of threat detection and response in critical infrastructure systems.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Industrial control systems (ICS) are critical networks directly linked to the value of core national and societal assets, yet they are increasingly becoming primary targets for numerous cyberattacks today. The ICS network, a fusion of operational technology (OT) and information technology (IT) networks, possesses a broad attack vector, and attacks targeting ICS often take the form of advanced persistent threats (APTs) exploiting zero-day vulnerabilities. However, most existing ICS security techniques have been adaptations of security technologies for IT networks, and security measures tailored to the characteristics of ICS data are currently insufficient. To mitigate cyber threats to ICS networks, this paper proposes an anomaly detection technique based on dynamic data abstraction. The proposed method abstracts ICS data collected in real time using a dynamic data abstraction technique based on noise reduction. The abstracted data are then used to optimize both the update rate and the detection accuracy of the anomaly detection model through model adaptation and incremental learning processes. The proposed approach updates the model by quickly reflecting data on new attack patterns and their distributions, effectively shortening the dwell time in response to APTs utilizing zero-day vulnerabilities. We demonstrate the attack response performance and detection accuracy of the proposed dynamic data abstraction-based anomaly detection technique through experiments using the SWaT dataset generated from a testbed of an actual ICS process. The experiments show that the proposed model achieves high accuracy with a small number of abstracted data while rapidly learning new attack pattern data in real-time without compromising accuracy. The proposed technique can effectively respond to cyberattacks targeting ICS by quickly learning and reflecting trends in attack patterns that exploit zero-day vulnerabilities.</jats:p>
title: Dynamic Data Abstraction-Based Anomaly Detection for Industrial Control Systems

items.abstract: <jats:p>Deep learning-based anomaly detection is effective for Industrial Control System time-series data, particularly with Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (Bi-LSTM) autoencoders. However, training on long-horizon datasets is memory-intensive and relies on offline batch training using the entire historical dataset at once. This requires all data to be processed simultaneously, limiting scalability, retraining flexibility, and practical usability on modest computational resources.This study proposed a statistically guided, selective incremental learning scheme for Bi-LSTM autoencoders, that reduced redundant retraining while preserving detection performance. Instead of batch training on the entire dataset, the model was updated incrementally using sequential chunks of normal-operation data, eliminating the need to store the complete dataset in memory. Anomaly detection used reconstruction error evaluated against fixed thresholds. To further improve training efficiency, a statistical similarity analysis identified and discarded highly redundant data chunks, reducing unnecessary updates without degrading detection capability.The proposed Selective incremental strategy was evaluated on the Secure Water Treatment (SWaT) and Water Distribution (WaDi) datasets, reducing Graphics Processing Unit Video Random Access Memory (GPU VRAM) consumption by 85% and 50--62% and training time by 46% and 31% respectively. Moreover, it achieved the best F1-score on SWaT (0.75), outperforming incremental (0.733) and vanilla batch-trained (0.74) baselines, while a comparable F1-score on WaDi (0.31--0.33) due to its higher dimensionality, confirming that the proposed approach preserved detection capability while delivering substantial resource savings. These results demonstrated that redundancy-aware incremental training provides a practical and scalable alternative for deep temporal anomaly detection across ICS datasets of varying complexity.</jats:p>
title: Redundancy-Aware Incremental Learning for Scalable Anomaly Detection in Resource-Constrained Industrial Control Systems
